newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand again denies besieged baht to be devalued.
newsitem.headline: Thailand again denies besieged baht to be devalued.

text.p: Thailand's central bank on Thursday denied again that the tumbling baht would be devalued amid heavy selling by mainly offshore speculators.

"The Bank of Thailand is monitoring the baht market very closely and will take necessary measures to stabilise the value of the baht," Bandid Nijathaworn, director of the central bank's banking department, told Reuters.
"We also wish to deny the rumours in the market about the baht devaluation," he said, declining to detail what specific action might be taken to defend it.
The baht, which was traded at around 25.90 early on Thursday, had lost nearly 10 satang by late afternoon to 26 per dollar after the offshore attacks on the currency.
The BOT had fixed the baht/dollar midrate at 25.87, a 6-1/2 year low on Thursday.
At 1003 GMT, the baht was bid/offered at 25.970/25.990 against the dollar.
Dealers said the devaluation rumours spread from New York and Singapore and sparked the attacks on the baht which has been steadily falling against the rallying dollar.

"The attack on the baht was launched because there are people who believe that the its value should be lower as economic conditions in the country are not as good as they should be," said a senior dealer with a foreign bank.
"It was also aimed at testing the resolve of the Thai central bank in defending the baht," he added.
The central bank released key monthly economic indicators on Thursday which showed that the balance of payments account had fallen sharply for the second month in a row.
It also said that the government's cash balance deficit widened to an estimated 30.3 billion baht in December 1996.
Forex dealers said that these negative data showed that the sluggish Thai economy would take more time to recover than previously expected.
Speculators used this as an excuse to attack the baht, they added.

In contrast, the Thai stock market welcomed some other central bank data which showed sharp narrowings of the Thai November 1996 current account and trade deficits which have been viewed with concern by some investors.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand's main index ended up nearly one percent at 820.18 points.

Dealers also said they believed there were two rounds of central bank intervention in the offshore markets to curb the baht's slide against the dollar, involving spending of up to $800 million to defend it.
